artwork.back: STAR Development Centre special edition SE01. Football in exile. 2021. After the Taliban returned to power, players were evacuated from Afghanistan. 2022. The team returned to football in Melbourne. 2026. A FIFA rule change opened the way to official international matches.

name: Afghanistan Women’s National Team
subtitle: Football in exile
story:
In August 2021, the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan. Women and girls lost the freedom to play organised football. Members of the Afghanistan women’s national team were among the footballers and other athletes evacuated to Australia. Former captain Khalida Popal helped players find a way to safety.

In 2022, players began training together again in Melbourne. Melbourne Victory supported their return to the pitch, and the team entered local competition in Victoria. Playing together helped them keep their team and their Afghan identity alive while they rebuilt their lives.

In 2025, Afghan Women United brought together Afghan footballers living outside the country. They played at a FIFA series in Morocco. In April 2026, FIFA changed its rules to allow Afghan women to represent their country in official international matches. This followed years of advocacy by players and their supporters.
facts: 2021 · Afghan footballers and other athletes were evacuated as the Taliban returned to power.
2022 · Players trained together again in Melbourne with Melbourne Victory’s support.
2026 · FIFA changed its rules to make official international representation possible.

artwork.back: STAR Development Centre special edition SE02. DPR Korea. 2001, 2003 and 2008. AFC Women’s Asian Cup champions. 2007. Women’s World Cup quarter-finalists. 2026. Qualified for the 2027 Women’s World Cup.

name: North Korea Women’s National Team
subtitle: Three Asian titles and a World Cup return
story:
North Korea’s senior women’s team competes internationally as DPR Korea. It won the AFC Women’s Asian Cup in 2001, 2003 and 2008. The team’s best FIFA Women’s World Cup finish came in 2007 in China. A 2–0 win over Nigeria helped it reach the quarter-finals.

In March 2026, DPR Korea faced Chinese Taipei in a World Cup qualifying play-off on Australia’s Gold Coast. Hong Song Ok scored three goals in a 4–0 win that secured a place at Brazil 2027. It will be the team’s first Women’s World Cup since Germany 2011.
facts: 2001, 2003 and 2008 · AFC Women’s Asian Cup champions.
2007 · FIFA Women’s World Cup quarter-finalists.
2026 · Beat Chinese Taipei 4–0 to qualify for Brazil 2027.

artwork.front: STAR Development Centre special edition SE03. Margaret Flett of Holm Ladies, Orkney, photographed in 1947 aged approximately 14. Heritage-gold illustrated card featuring her quartered football kit and the 1947 team behind her.
artwork.back: STAR Development Centre special edition SE03. Holm Ladies Football Team, Holm in Orkney, 1947. Eleven known players from a surviving team photograph. A recollection of a match with Kirkwall Ladies survives.

name: Margaret Flett & Holm Ladies
subtitle: A girl from Orkney's forgotten football team
story:
In 1947, eleven women and girls from Holm in Orkney posed together for a photograph. They wore striking dark-and-light football shirts, some with skirts and others with shorts. Behind them stood old cars; in the front row, the woman in the middle held a ball marked “HOLM LADIES 1947”. The photograph gives us a rare glimpse of local women's football in the years after the Second World War.

Kneeling at the far left of the front row was Margaret Flett. She is believed to have been about fourteen years old. She is remembered as a very fast, agile player, although surviving match records do not allow us to measure her performances or reconstruct her playing career. In the photograph she faces the camera in her quartered shirt and dark shorts: a young footballer who belonged to a team.

We know the names of the other players because people who recognised the photograph helped identify them. The back row is recorded as Elaine Crowther, Sally Peterson, Elma Kirkness, Lil Anderson, Janet Mair and Violet Flett. Alongside Margaret in the front row were Margaret Buchan, Madge Garriock, Elsie Buchan and Vera Garriock. Their names are an important part of the team's surviving history. Despite sharing a surname, we cannot confirm whether Margaret and Violet Flett were related.

One contributor to the Orkney Image Library remembered Kirkwall Ladies visiting Holm and winning 10–0. This is a community recollection, not a verified contemporary match report. We do not yet know how many matches Holm played, how long the team lasted, or what Margaret did later in life.

The mystery is part of why this card matters. Football history is not only about famous internationals and trophies. It also belongs to the girls who pulled on a shirt and played for their local community, even when few people wrote down their achievements. Margaret and her teammates deserve to be remembered.
facts: 1947 · A surviving photograph records the Holm Ladies Football Team in Orkney.
Margaret Flett · Identified at the far left of the front row; believed to be about fourteen.
11 players · Their names were identified through local archive contributions.
Kirkwall match · A 10–0 score survives as an unverified community recollection.

artwork.front: STAR Football History special edition. Robbins Gloving Factory Ladies, Yeovil, Somerset, circa 1936. Illustrated reconstruction of women playing in period football kits, framed by stitched leather and a robin.
artwork.back: Robbins Gloving Factory Ladies, Yeovil, Somerset, circa 1936. From factory to football. Glove factory workers in Alexandra Road played for a cup-winning team. Look closely at the shirts and you’ll see a robin. Illustrated reconstruction based on the South Somerset Heritage Collection team photograph.

name: Robbins Gloving Factory Ladies
subtitle: From the glove factory to the football pitch
story:
Look closely at the surviving team photograph and you can see a small robin on the players’ shirts. Some hold trophies and one holds a football. Somerset Council lists the photograph under 1936, while the Community Heritage Access Centre dates it to around the mid-1930s.

Several of the women worked at Edwin ‘Tink’ Robbins’ glove factory on Alexandra Road in Yeovil. The South Somerset Heritage Collection records that Edwin organised games and that the team won a cup. The Community Heritage Access Centre identifies him in the back row of the photograph.

The club’s bird is the detail that makes this team instantly recognisable. It links the women’s football shirts to the name of the factory where they worked. The surviving sources used here leave the name of the cup and the final score open.
facts: Yeovil · The glove factory stood on Alexandra Road.
Mid-1930s · Somerset Council lists the team photograph under 1936.
A robin · The bird appears on the team’s shirts.
Cup winners · The heritage collection records that the team won a cup.

artwork.front: STAR Football History special edition SE05. Bath Ladies AFC. Old Trafford, 1921. Illustrated reconstruction of players in hockey-style kit beside a packed terrace.
artwork.back: Bath Ladies AFC. 24 names in silver. In June 1922, the club presented a silver case to Alfred Edward Manns. It carries the names of 24 players and officials. Illustrated reconstruction inspired by the case featured by the National Football Museum.

name: Bath Ladies AFC
subtitle: From Bath to a packed Old Trafford
story:
In 1921, Bath Ladies AFC played Dick, Kerr Ladies of Preston at Old Trafford. The National Football Museum estimates that between 25,000 and 30,000 people watched. Between 1920 and 1921 Bath played at least ten games and raised more than £3,000 for post-war charities.

Dorothy Harrison served as captain and vice-captain at different times. Her sisters Edie, Mabel and Audley played alongside her. The team's distinctive hockey-style kit appears in surviving photographs, including pictures from their match against Plymouth.

In June 1922, the players and officials presented their honorary secretary and treasurer, Alfred Edward Manns, with a silver case. Its reverse carries 24 names. The engraving preserves the names of people who helped make the team possible.
facts: Old Trafford · Bath played Dick, Kerr Ladies in 1921.
25,000–30,000 · Estimated crowd at Old Trafford.
Dorothy Harrison · Played alongside three of her sisters.
24 names · Engraved on the silver case presented in 1922.

artwork.front: STAR Football History special edition SE06. Keynsham Super Strikers, founded 1993. Illustrated reconstruction of girls playing football in green and white.
artwork.back: From Super Strikers to Keynsham Town Ladies. In 1993, girls from Chandag Primary started the Super Strikers and played under-11 six-a-side football. In 1998/99 the team became Keynsham Town Ladies and joined the South West Women’s League. Illustrated reconstruction.

name: Keynsham Super Strikers
subtitle: The schoolgirls who started a club
story:
In 1993, girls from Chandag Primary asked Barrie Newton to help them start a football team. They called themselves the Super Strikers and played in a local under-11 six-a-side league.

They played six-a-side for about three years. As more players joined, the team started playing occasional eleven-a-side friendlies. Local telecommunications company Protel sponsored the club, which took the name Protel Super Strikers and adopted a green-and-white kit during this period.

In 1998/99 the team took the name Keynsham Town Ladies FC, entered Division Two of the South West Women’s League and finished third. The front illustrates the early story with imagined players and uses green and white as a nod to the kit adopted later.
facts: 1993 · Girls from Chandag Primary founded the Super Strikers.
Under-11 · They started in a local six-a-side league.
Protel · A local sponsor gave the team its second name.
1998/99 · Keynsham Town Ladies finished third in Division Two.
